title: DiffRatio: Training One-Step Diffusion Models Without Teacher Supervision
claim: Our method estimates the score difference far more accurately than the baseline across all noise levels on a controlled toy problem.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared log-scale noise axis, ours vs baseline
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a log-scale x-axis of noise level sigma, from 10^-1 to about 20. The left panel, titled 'Normalized L2 Error (Lower is better)', uses a log y-axis. The right panel, titled 'Cosine Similarity (Higher is better)', uses a linear y-axis. Each panel has two series. DiffRatio is a blue line with circle markers. VSD is an orange line with triangle markers. In the left panel, VSD error starts high at small sigma and falls to about 1, then rises again. DiffRatio stays below it at every sigma and reaches its minimum near sigma 10. In the right panel, DiffRatio's cosine similarity rises to about 0.9, while VSD stays well below it and starts slightly negative. Titles state which direction is better, and a legend sits in the upper corner of each panel.
caption: Score difference estimation accuracy on a 2D mixture of Gaussians problem.
abstract: Score-based distillation methods train one-step diffusion models in two stages: they first train a teacher score model, then distill it into a one-step student model. However, this distillation process can introduce bias from two sources: errors in the teacher score model and student score estimate. We propose DiffRatio, a new approach for training one-step diffusion models without teacher supervision based on a density-ratio formulation that connects score-based distribution matching and GAN-style adversarial training. Instead of using a teacher score model to provide training targets, DiffRatio directly learns a log density ratio between the student and data distributions across diffusion time steps. As a pre-trained score model is only used to initialize the one-step generator and does not supervise training, this design simplifies the training pipeline, mitigates gradient estimation bias, and reduces the size of auxiliary networks. The learned density ratio can be used as a verifier, enabling a principled inference-time parallel scaling method that further improves sample quality without external rewards or extra sequential computation. DiffRatio achieves strong one-step generation results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet (64x64 and 512x512), outperforming most teacher-supervised distillation methods.
